captions.text: I'm Kali, and this is DAF-18
of my Delhi Air Forecast project.
Honestly, this ticket confused me at first.
So let me explain it the way I
finally understood it, with a school story.
See, there is a school in Delhi,
and the coordinator is Asha madam.
Delhi's air is sometimes very bad.
The tiny dust is measured as PM2.5,
and ninety-one or more is called Poor.
On a Poor day,
children should not stand outside.
So every evening she must decide:
tomorrow morning, will six hundred children
stand outside for assembly, or stay indoors?
For that, she needs a guess
of tomorrow's PM2.5.
Now, she has two ways to guess.
Way one, her old method, persistence:
look at today's reading and say
tomorrow will be the same.
It is free.
Way two, a small machine-learning model
called Ridge, which looks at today,
and the last three, seven and fourteen days.
So the whole project asks one question:
is the model really better
than the free method?
Because if not, why keep the computer?
Let's see where she is.
In the earlier tickets,
she built the model, like learning
the chapters and writing practice tests.
In DAF-17, she chose the settings using
only her two hundred fifty-one study days,
and signed her final plan in a file.
Now, in DAF-18, she opens the one hundred
thirty test days, from the first of March.
This is the real board exam paper.
Here's the catch.
Those test days are locked
in a sealed envelope.
The model has never learned from them.
That is exactly why they
can give an honest answer.
Left of this line, the model may study.
Right of it, only judge.
Now think about the temptation.
She opens the envelope, sees a poor score,
quietly changes one setting,
and opens it again.
The score looks better.
But now the test days have started teaching
the model, so the score is a lie.
The rule is simple: open the envelope once.
And before she opens it, the principal
writes the pass marks on the board.
Otherwise, you write
the marks that suit you.
Rule one: the average mistake,
called MAE, must be at least ten
percent lower than persistence.
Rule two: it must catch
at least as many Poor days.
Both must hold, right?
And honestly, in the practice tests,
the win was only three point eight percent.
So the answer may well be: not met.
Let's see it on a toy town,
with twenty-two made-up readings.
Each row is a question:
today is this, what is tomorrow?
Fourteen rows are study rows,
seven are sealed.
Ridge learns only from the study rows,
and finds a rule: tomorrow equals zero
point three times today, plus sixty-five.
Basically, a very high day
is usually followed by a lower one.
The old method cannot
know that.
Now she opens the envelope, once.
Same seven rows for both methods,
otherwise it is unfair.
Each stick is a mistake.
Persistence is off by eighteen point
six on average, Ridge by fifteen.
That is nineteen percent better.
Both methods catch three of four Poor days.
Both rules met.
But look, Ridge does not win every row.
MAE looks at the average.
One exam can be luck,
so she also checks smaller monthly
exams inside the study days.
This is called walk-forward.
In the real project,
Ridge scored thirty point four,
against about thirty-five for persistence.
If it had disagreed,
she would not change anything.
She would write
the disagreement in the report.
A good student does not only count marks.
She opens the answer sheet.
Which days did the model lose most?
In the toy, the air suddenly
cleaned up overnight, and nothing
in today's number warned about it.
In a long smog spell,
Ridge guessed too low.
These are patterns, so the ten worst
days go into the report as failure cases.
Last, she saves the model
in one file with joblib.
New session, nothing in memory,
load it back, and check: the same day
gives one hundred point seven before,
and one hundred point seven after.
Then comes the model card,
like the paper inside a medicine box:
what it is for, the data,
how good it is, where it fails,
and when not to use it.
It must also say that the test days
were already peeked at earlier.
So, basically, as Java developers,
this should feel familiar.
The test set is data you
never touch while developing.
The pass marks are acceptance
criteria written first.
The model file is the build the service
loads, and the model card is the README.
DAF-18 is not about making the model better.
It is about testing it once, and reporting
honestly, even if the result is bad.
DAF-18 done.
Next: DAF-19, the live service.
